message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – processes many similar operations at once. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (2–32 on consumer chips). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores. |
| **Execution style** | Serial/low‑latency – each core can handle complex branching and decision making. | SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) – many cores execute the same instruction on different data simultaneously. |
| **Clock speed** | High clock speeds (≈3 GHz+) because each core does heavy work. | Lower clock speeds (≈1 GHz) because each core is simpler. |
| **Cache & memory** | Large L1/L2 caches per core; sophisticated memory hierarchy. | Smaller per‑core cache; relies on high‑bandwidth shared memory. |
| **Instruction set** | Complex, with many control flow instructions. | Simple, often limited to arithmetic and data movement. |
| **Typical workloads** | Running operating systems, web browsers, office apps, database engines, etc. | Rendering images, video decoding, scientific simulations, machine‑learning inference/training. |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for single‑thread performance. | Optimized for throughput; many cores share power efficiently. |

In short, a CPU excels at tasks that require strong single‑thread performance and complex logic, while a GPU shines when you can break a problem into many identical, independent operations that can run in parallel.
